study.title: Psalm 50 - God judges religion empty and welcomes true worship
study.overview: This psalm presents God as Judge who summons the whole earth, examines his people and denounces both confidence in heartless rituals and moral hypocrisy. The text does not reject the sacrifice itself, but corrects the false idea that God depends on him or that he replaces gratitude, repentance, obedience, and justice. At the end, the way approved is that of whom it offers praise, lives in an ordained way and seeks the salvation of God.

outline.title: God summons creation to judge
outline.explanation: The first verses describe the Lord as the universal Judge who speaks, calls the whole earth and appears in majesty. Heavens and earth are gathered as witnesses, and the center of the scene is God Himself, who comes to establish justice among his people.

outline.title: The Lord corrects his people on sacrifice and worship
outline.explanation: God remembers the covenant with Israel, but clarifies that he does not accuse him of lack of animal offerings. He shows that he does not need food or human goods; the worship he desires is gratitude, fulfillment of vows and crying out in the day of anguish, with promise of deliverance.

outline.title: The wicked is denounced, and the faithful is guided to true salvation
outline.explanation: Now the word is addressed to the ungodly who uses the mouth to speak of God, but rejects his instruction and practices injustice, adultery, lies, and defamation. God will not remain silent forever; there will be judgment. In contrast, what glorifies Him is the sacrifice of praise and the watchful life, and this path leads to the salvation of God.

study.context: The psalm is attributed to Asaph and functions as a word of public instruction and rebuke. The notes provided highlight that it was composed to confront trust in external religious practices without practical pity. They also show that the initial scene has court language, with God calling heaven and earth as witnesses against the infidelity of his people.
study.theology: The central message is that God is not impressed with external religiosity when an obedient heart is lacking. The sacrifice does not buy divine favor, for everything already belongs to the Lord; therefore, true worship involves praise, gratitude, repentance, trust and integrity. The psalm also states that God's patience does not eliminate judgment: divine silence is not approval. For those who believe, the righteousness of God is comforting; for the hypocrites, it is a warning. The conclusion unites worship and ethics: glorifying God includes walking correctly, and salvation comes from God Himself, not from mere religious form.

scholarViews.insight: The Psalm teaches that the ritual performance and the recitation of the law are useless without gratitude, repentance and justice; at first, all creation is summoned to pay attention when God approaches to bring justice to the world.
The psalm is a word of instruction and rebuke: God treats, first, with those who rested in external observances and then with those who had made religion only one appearance, without practical pity.
The final blessing belongs to those who offer praise and walks correctly; the commentator connects this to the path of those who worship God truly and live without guilt before him.

questions: In which areas can I be relying more on external religious practice than in a grateful and obedient heart?
Is my way of speaking of God consistent with my way of treating others, or is there hypocrisy between my mouth and my actions?
When I go through anguish, I first seek God in sincere cry, or just desire relief without transformation?
study.practice: This week, take time to thank God in a concrete way, mentioning specific blessings and renewing before him the commitments you have made. At the same time, examine your relationships: abandon an attitude of lies, unjust criticism or connivance with sin, and practice visible obedience. If there is a need, seek someone mature in the faith to confess an incoherence and ask for prayer. Turn praise into life: thank God with your lips and straight choices.
study.uncertainty: The text and notes allow us to safely affirm that the psalm confronts religious hypocrisy and exalts obedient praise, but do not allow detailing dates, specific place of composition or accurately identify the exact historical situation. There are also different confessional readings in the notes, especially on the relationship between the Old Testament sacrifices and their later application; therefore, these connections must be understood as interpretation, not as explicit detail of the psalm.
